summary: In this episode, Fr. Andrew and Fr. Stephen explore the resurrection appearances of Christ, arguing that they are not merely evidence for the resurrection but revelations of Christ's divine identity as Yahweh, the God of Israel, who has come to visit His people. They connect the concept of 'anastasis' (resurrection) to the Old Testament 'Day of the Lord,' a day of judgment and restoration when God arises to set things right. The hosts emphasize that the resurrection appearances are part of the gospel itself, as seen in St. Paul's list in 1 Corinthians 15, and that they reveal Christ's glory, making the disciples apostles sent on a mission. The episode also addresses common misunderstandings, such as viewing the resurrection as mere resuscitation, and highlights the liturgical context of these readings in the Sunday Matins service. The second half includes caller questions on the nature of hell and the value of historical-critical scholarship, while the third half delves into specific appearances: to the Myrrhbearers, St. Peter, St. James, the 500, and St. Paul. The hosts conclude by urging listeners to seek the face of Christ in Scripture and liturgy, and to respond to that vision by going out into the world to transform it.

entities.title: Jesus Christ
entities.summary: The central figure of Christianity, identified as Yahweh the God of Israel who visits His people. His resurrection is the Anastasis, the Day of the Lord.

entities.title: St. Paul the Apostle
entities.summary: Apostle who lists resurrection appearances in 1 Corinthians 15, emphasizing their importance. He describes himself as 'one born out of time' (abortion) in humility.

entities.title: St. Peter
entities.summary: Apostle who denied Christ three times and was restored by Christ asking 'Do you love me?' three times. His restoration contrasts with Judas.

entities.title: St. James the Brother of the Lord
entities.summary: First bishop of Jerusalem, who did not believe during Christ's ministry but was converted by a resurrection appearance and put in charge of the Jerusalem church.

entities.title: Myrrhbearers
entities.summary: The women who first discovered the empty tomb and were the first to see the risen Christ, becoming apostles to the apostles. Their role highlights God's pattern of using the lowly.

concepts.title: Anastasis (Resurrection)
concepts.summary: The Greek word for resurrection, used specifically for Christ's rising, which is not a mere resuscitation but a cosmic event inaugurating the Day of the Lord. It signifies God arising to judge and restore creation.

concepts.title: Day of the Lord
concepts.summary: An Old Testament concept of Yahweh visiting His creation to establish justice, involving judgment on heavenly and earthly powers, and the resurrection of the righteous. This day is inaugurated at Christ's crucifixion and resurrection.

concepts.title: Resurrection Appearances as Revelation
concepts.summary: The post-resurrection appearances of Christ are not primarily evidence for the resurrection but revelations of His divine identity as Lord of glory, making the disciples apostles.

concepts.title: Prophetic Commission and Apostleship
concepts.summary: The resurrection appearances function like prophetic commissions in the Old Testament, where the seer is sent (apostello) on a mission. This makes the apostles those who have seen the Lord and are sent.

claims.text: Christ's resurrection is not a resuscitation like Lazarus; it is a different event—the Anastasis—inaugurating the Day of the Lord and the new creation.
The Day of the Lord prophesied in the Old Testament occurs at Christ's crucifixion and resurrection, as shown by the darkening of the sun and the rising of saints.
The resurrection appearances are not presented as legal evidence; they are revelations of Christ's divine identity. The fact that people often fail to recognize Him undercuts an evidential reading.
The first witnesses to the resurrection are women, which would be counterproductive as propaganda in the ancient world, but fits God's pattern of exalting the lowly.

scriptural_links.summary: Describes the Day of the Lord when heavenly forces and earthly kings are imprisoned, then punished after many days—used to show the timing of judgment.
Many saints rise after Christ's resurrection, connecting to the Day of the Lord and the harrowing of hell.
Jesus tells Martha 'I am the resurrection and the life,' identifying Himself as the Anastasis and the God of Israel who visits His people.
St. Paul lists resurrection appearances as part of the gospel, emphasizing that Christ was seen by many, not as evidence but as revelation.

glossary.definition: Greek for 'resurrection,' specifically Christ's rising, which is the inauguration of the Day of the Lord and the restoration of all things.
The eleven resurrection gospel readings used in Sunday Matins, proclaimed facing north as a victory announcement against God's enemies.
A psalm verse chanted before the gospel reading in Matins, often calling on God to arise (anastasis) and judge the earth.
